channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Trump offered to help end the Russia-Ukraine war after a 90-minute call with Putin and a separate call with Zelensky, who saw a "real prospect" of peace — but heavy Russian air attacks on Kyiv and Sumy continue in parallel.
item.description:
On 4-5 July, Trump held a 90-minute call with Putin and then spoke with Zelensky, offering to help broker an end to the war. Zelensky described a "real prospect" of ending the conflict. The overture lands just before the NATO summit in Ankara on 7-8 July, giving the initiative a concrete near-term test. The diplomatic signal contrasts sharply with events on the ground: a Russian missile strike on Kyiv killed 30 people, and further strikes on Sumy and Kyiv regions used 105 drones and two missiles in a single night. Zelensky's priority in his call with Chancellor Merz was Patriot air-defence missiles — supply of which is constrained because the US-Iran war depleted stocks.

For the chemical and ACS industry, the stakes are two-sided. A credible ceasefire would ease European energy prices, begin unwinding sanctions, and eventually open very large reconstruction demand for construction materials, adhesives, sealants, and coatings. Continued escalation sustains defence-industrial demand but keeps energy and risk premia elevated. The IMF has already cut Ukraine's 2026 growth forecast to 1-1.6%, with output near 80% of pre-war levels — and explicitly cited the Iran war and Hormuz closure as additional drags. Benchmarked against past conflict-resolution attempts, a leader-to-leader channel is a necessary but far-from-sufficient condition; execution risk is high.

Al Jazeera | The Guardian | The Independent | Handelsblatt | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: The US-Iran war caused the largest-ever oil supply shock by volume; Gulf petrochemical and fertiliser flows and Japan's naphtha supply were hit, and Iran now plans Hormuz transit fees — with a discount for China.
item.description:
Reuters reports the war produced the largest oil supply shock ever measured by volume, though total economic losses still trail the 1979 shock. The temporary closure of the Strait of Hormuz — the transit point for a fifth of global oil and much Gulf LNG — paralysed not just crude but the region's petrochemical and fertiliser ecosystem, per Dawn's analysis. The downstream effect reached manufacturers directly: a naphtha squeeze in Japan pushed food makers to substitute away from plastic packaging. Asia, the most import-dependent region, is already drawing lessons and building strategic reserves. Iran now plans to charge ships transiting Hormuz, offering China preferential terms — a sign the disruption is shifting from acute to structural.

For chemical and ACS producers, naphtha and crude are the primary cost anchors for polymers, resins, and solvents used across adhesives, coatings, and sealants. The direction of travel is favourable — Ifo attributes the June rebound in German chemical sentiment (see insight 11) to easing energy and input prices as the crisis de-escalates. But the transmission lag from crude to formulated-product cost is typically three to six months, so meaningful margin relief will arrive in Q3-Q4 2026. The lasting risk is a structurally higher Gulf-transit cost embedded in feedstock logistics, plus renewed dependence on stable maritime passage.

Reuters | Dawn | The Economic Times | Cnyes | Hong Kong Economic Times

item.title: Merz's coalition presented 34 measures — about €10 billion in annual tax relief, pension reform, day-one sick notes, deregulation, and explicit support for chemicals, autos, AI, and clean tech. The DAX hit a record; leading institutes call it insufficient.
item.description:
On 2 July, Chancellor Merz's coalition unveiled a "programme for growth and employment": roughly €10 billion in annual income-tax relief for lower and middle earners (from 2027), a pension-system overhaul, a requirement for a doctor's note from day one of illness, an 8% cut in federal-ministry staffing through digitisation, and a red-tape reduction drive. Notably, the package names automotive, chemicals, AI, and clean technology as sectors for explicit support. Markets responded immediately — the DAX set a record 25,810 points for a second consecutive day on reform optimism.

The professional verdict is more sober. The Ifo Institute, DIW Berlin, ZEW Mannheim, and the Kiel Institute jointly concluded the package will not be enough to pull Germany out of its long-standing crisis, and Handelsblatt analysis argues the headline tax relief shrinks sharply for household types other than the dual-earner family used as the government's example. The reforms address demand and labour-market flexibility more than the supply-side roots — high energy costs, deindustrialisation, and weak investment. For Henkel and other German chemical producers, lower taxes, reduced bureaucracy, and explicit sector recognition improve the operating climate at the margin; the decisive variable is implementation speed before the summer recess, and whether energy costs are tackled next.

Deutsche Welle | MarketScreener | Handelsblatt — Economists | Handelsblatt — DAX | Japan Today

item.title: The US declined to extend USMCA, shifting to annual reviews and citing Chinese content routed through Mexico. Manufacturers face rolling uncertainty; Canada — which sends about 70% of exports to the US — is most exposed, and analysts cut its currency forecasts.
item.description:
Rather than confirming the long extension businesses expected, the US moved USMCA onto an annual-review footing. The Alliance for American Manufacturing pressed for tighter rules of origin to capture upstream inputs and block Chinese content entering via Mexican-assembled vehicles — the central US grievance. Because the agreement stays in force but without multi-year certainty, companies must now re-evaluate North American manufacturing footprints every twelve months against shifting US demands. Analysts responded by cutting Canadian-dollar forecasts, noting Canada routes roughly 70% of its exports to the US and that the uncertainty also reduces the odds of Bank of Canada rate moves.

For the chemical and ACS industry, USMCA's zero-tariff framework underpins integrated North American supply chains for polymer resins, adhesive raw materials, and specialty intermediates, and the automotive assembly base that consumes them. A rolling review cycle raises hedging costs and deters long-term capacity investment on the continent. Benchmarked against the 2018 NAFTA renegotiation, which resolved in about 13 months, the annual-review format is structurally more destabilising precisely because it never resolves — uncertainty becomes the permanent state. Manufacturers with Mexican exposure face the sharpest planning risk.

South China Morning Post | MarketScreener

item.title: The EU and China set an October deadline for deliverables on the €360bn trade imbalance, export controls, and IP. China guaranteed rare-earth and magnet export controls will not disrupt EU supply, while signalling openness to buy more EU goods.
item.description:
The two sides agreed to work toward concrete outcomes by October on the imbalance, export controls, and intellectual property, with China's Commerce Minister Wang Wentao signalling openness to purchase agreements covering EU goods. Critically for industry, China guaranteed that its rare-earth and magnet export controls would not disrupt EU supply — the single most important supply-security assurance in the package. Von der Leyen warned that dialogue "has to deliver on trade imbalances." The backdrop is stark: Goldman Sachs finds the EU's slowdown is driven more by market-share loss to China than by the deficit itself — Chinese exports to the EU rose about 16% in the first five months of 2026 while EU exports to China grew under 10%.

For chemical and ACS producers, two channels matter. First, rare earths and magnets are critical inputs for the electronics, EV, and machinery customers that buy adhesives and coatings; a credible supply guarantee reduces a major tail risk. Second, the EU is simultaneously weighing countervailing duties on Chinese EVs and possibly plug-in hybrids — a signal that trade friction will persist even as talks proceed. The realistic base case is managed friction rather than resolution: firms should treat the October milestone as a checkpoint, not a settlement.

Lianhe Zaobao | Hürriyet Daily News | Chinatimes | South China Morning Post | Commercial Times — Goldman

item.title: A German Economic Institute study shows EU-US goods trade reached a record €875bn in 2025, with a €285bn EU surplus. Yet EU car and parts exports to the US fell 20.4% (Germany -18.9%), while tariff-exempt pharma and chemicals lifted Ireland's exports 52.7%.
item.description:
The IW study captures a paradox: aggregate EU-US goods trade set a record at €875 billion in 2025, EU exports rose 7.7% to €580 billion, and the EU surplus widened to about €285 billion — all despite the tariff dispute. But the composition tells the real story. Tariffs bit hardest where they were applied: EU car and parts exports to the US fell 20.4%, with Germany down 18.9%. Meanwhile Ireland's exports surged 52.7%, driven by pharmaceuticals and chemicals that were largely tariff-exempt — a vivid illustration of how selective tariffs redirect rather than reduce trade.

For Henkel, the pattern is directly instructive. Chemical and adhesive product flows have so far been relatively shielded compared with automotive, but the company's largest customer sector — automotive — is absorbing a heavy tariff hit precisely in the transatlantic corridor. This compounds the German auto sector's existing pressure and signals softer OEM demand for ACS inputs on both sides of the Atlantic. Benchmarking across sectors, the divergence between shielded pharma/chemicals and exposed autos shows why tariff-line detail, not headline totals, should drive commercial planning. The record aggregate could also invite renewed US attention to the surplus itself.

MarketScreener | Dünya Gazetesi

item.title: The US plans to repeal 702 rules (~$1.5tn projected savings) including the EPA's GHG "endangerment finding," while the UK launches a carbon border tax (2027) and tighter chemical-emission rules, and Germany's new VAT decree undercuts the EU Critical Raw Materials Act.
item.description:
A structural transatlantic split is widening. In the US, the administration plans to cut 702 rules by September 2026, projecting roughly $1.5 trillion in savings, targeting energy-project environmental review, efficiency standards, and DEI — and moving to repeal the EPA's 2009 "endangerment finding," the legal foundation of federal greenhouse-gas regulation. In the opposite direction, the UK will launch its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism on 1 January 2027 covering aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, and iron and steel; the EU's CBAM is already raising supplier compliance costs; and a UNFCCC study models the trade and employment effects of border-carbon pricing. The UK is also tightening chemical-sector air-emission limits (Waste Gas for Chemicals) affecting some 300 sites by 2030. Meanwhile a German VAT decree now applies 19% VAT to bonded-warehouse raw-material transactions, prompting at least one dealer to shift 200 tonnes of rare earths and minerals to Switzerland — directly undercutting the EU's own Critical Raw Materials Act.

For chemical and ACS producers, this divergence reshapes competitiveness geographically. US operations face falling compliance costs and cheaper energy-linked inputs; EU/UK operations face rising carbon and emissions costs plus, in Germany, a self-inflicted raw-material logistics penalty. The strategic implication is a widening cost gap that favours US-based production and complicates EU raw-material sourcing — a factor for capacity-allocation and procurement decisions. Benchmarked historically, this is the sharpest regulatory divergence between the blocs in a decade.

The Economic Times — US Rules | Yahoo! France | TechUK — UK CBAM | The Economic Times — EU CBAM | UNFCCC | Neue Zürcher Zeitung — German VAT | CIA — UK Chemical BAT

item.title: A UN University report projects AI data centres will consume 945 TWh by 2030 (from 448 TWh in 2025), with a 9.3-trillion-litre water footprint. Morgan Stanley frames AI as a systemic shift spanning infrastructure, energy, robotics, and geopolitics.
item.description:
The UN University report puts a hard number on AI's physical cost: data centres powering AI will more than double electricity consumption to 945 TWh by 2030, with a water footprint of 9.3 trillion litres, threatening land and water resources for billions. Morgan Stanley Investment Management's Q2 2026 report, "AI: Ten Investment Truths," reframes AI as no longer a technology race but a systemic change spanning infrastructure, software, capital, energy, robotics, geopolitics, and corporate governance — with capital commitments that dwarf prior technology cycles.

For the chemical and ACS industry the read-through is concrete and mostly positive on the demand side. Data-centre construction at this scale drives demand for thermal-interface materials, electrically conductive and structural adhesives, sealants, and protective coatings used in servers, power electronics, and cooling systems. It also accelerates electronics-materials consumption broadly. The offsetting risk is energy: AI's power draw competes for the same electricity whose cost is a decisive input for energy-intensive chemical production, particularly in Europe. Benchmarked against previous digital build-outs, the distinguishing feature here is the coupling of compute growth with physical resource intensity — meaning AI expansion is now also a materials and energy story, not only a software one, and belongs on the industrial planning agenda.

AA — Anadolu Agency | Cnyes — Morgan Stanley

item.title: The UK, Italy, and Japan awarded a £4.6bn, 18-month contract to the Edgewing JV (BAE Systems, Leonardo, Mitsubishi/JAIEC) to advance the GCAP sixth-generation fighter, targeted for service in 2035. The UK committed £8.6bn over four years.
item.description:
The Global Combat Air Programme reached a concrete funding milestone with a £4.6 billion, 18-month development contract to Edgewing, the joint venture between BAE Systems, Italy's Leonardo, and Japan's Mitsubishi-led JAIEC. The UK has committed £8.6 billion over four years, with the aircraft targeted to enter service in 2035. GCAP sits within a broader rearmament wave across NATO members — the same dataset shows NATO moving to replace AWACS with Saab GlobalEye and elevated Patriot demand from the Ukraine and Iran conflicts — indicating a durable, multi-year defence-industrial upcycle.

For chemical and ACS producers, next-generation aerospace platforms are intensive users of high-performance structural adhesives, composite bonding systems, sealants, and specialty coatings — the higher-margin end of the portfolio, with long qualification cycles that reward early positioning. The trilateral UK-Italy-Japan structure also spreads demand across three priority regions. Benchmarked against legacy programmes, sixth-generation designs rely more heavily on advanced composites and bonded assemblies than riveted metal airframes, raising adhesive and coating content per aircraft. The main caveat is timeline: development-phase volumes are modest and real materials demand scales only as the programme approaches production toward the 2030s. The near-term value is strategic customer positioning, not immediate revenue.

The Economic Times | MarketScreener | JIJI Press

item.title: ECB President Lagarde did not rule out leaving before her October 2027 term ends, potentially to contest the April 2027 French presidential election. With Macron term-limited and the Rassemblement National leading polls, this injects monetary-policy and political-risk uncertainty.
item.description:
Lagarde said she cannot exclude an early departure from the ECB, openly linking it to the possibility of entering the French political arena. Her term runs to October 2027; the French presidential election is in April 2027, and Macron cannot run again. With the Rassemblement National leading polls, the prospect raises two distinct risks. The first is monetary-policy continuity: a mid-cycle leadership change at the ECB during a period of easing inflation (Eurozone CPI has cooled toward 2.8%) and delicate rate calibration would introduce uncertainty into the euro-area rate path. The second is political: a Lagarde candidacy would signal the centre's fear of an RN victory, sharpening France's — and the EU's — political-risk premium.

For the chemical and ACS industry, the euro-area interest-rate path directly shapes construction and industrial-investment demand — the end markets for adhesives, coatings, and sealants. Leadership uncertainty at the ECB, combined with French political risk in the bloc's second-largest economy, argues for caution on the timing and pace of any European demand recovery. Benchmarked against prior central-bank transitions, markets typically tolerate planned successions but react poorly to unplanned or politically charged exits — making this a watch item rather than an immediate market mover.

Handelsblatt | Il Sole 24 Ore | La Repubblica

item.title: US June payrolls rose just 57,000 (vs ~110,000 expected) as 700,000 left the workforce, pushing the Fed toward a hold. German chemical sentiment jumped to -17.8 (Ifo), China's PMI held expansion at 50.3, and Japan's wage deals averaged 5.01%.
item.description:
The global demand signal is mixed but coherent. In the US, June payrolls rose only 57,000 against expectations near 110,000, with unemployment falling to 4.2% only because roughly 700,000 people left the workforce (participation 61.5%, the lowest since 2021). Markets cut July rate-hike odds below 20%, keeping the Fed range at 3.50-3.75%, and Eurozone CPI cooled toward 2.8%. In Germany, the Ifo business-climate index for the chemical industry improved sharply from -29.0 in May to -17.8 in June, with current conditions at -2.9 and expectations at -31.5 — Ifo credits easing energy and input prices after Middle East de-escalation. In Asia, China's manufacturing PMI held expansion at 50.3 for a fourth month (high-tech sub-index 53.5), and Japan's largest union group confirmed average wage rises of 5.01%, a third straight year above 5%, supporting the BoJ's normalisation path.

For Henkel, the German chemical-sentiment rebound is the single most on-point indicator — it confirms the feedstock-cost relief thesis from insight 2 is already lifting sector confidence, even if levels remain negative. The picture points to gradually improving European chemical conditions, resilient Chinese industrial demand, and firm Japanese domestic demand, set against a cooling US that may soften North American volumes into H2. Benchmarked against Q1, the direction in Europe is the encouraging change.

Reuters — US Fed | MarketScreener — US Jobs | The Economic Times — CPI | ChemEurope — Ifo | China Economic Net — PMI | MarketScreener — Japan Wages

item.title: China's Circular Economy 15th Five-Year Plan targets the world's largest recycling system by 2030 — CNY 8tn recycling output and 4.5bn tonnes of solid-waste use — while a new mandatory packaging standard limiting sealing tape took effect on 1 July.
item.description:
Two Chinese policy moves converge on materials and packaging. The NDRC's Circular Economy 15th Five-Year Plan aims to build the world's largest circular-economy system by 2030, with recycling output of CNY 8 trillion, 4.5 billion tonnes of solid-waste utilisation, and expanded recycling of EV batteries, wind, and PV components — plus an explicit push to increase use of recycled materials. Separately, a mandatory national standard for express-delivery packaging took effect on 1 July, imposing three-tier limits on box adaptation, packaging layers, and sealing-tape use in the world's largest e-commerce logistics market.

For the ACS industry these are directly relevant, with mixed implications. The packaging standard constrains sealing-tape volume per parcel — a headwind for the adhesive-tape segment in China's vast parcel market, though partly offset by continued e-commerce growth. The circular-economy plan is the more strategic signal: mandated recycled-content use reshapes feedstock streams and will require adhesives and coatings formulated for recyclability and for bonding recycled substrates — a design-for-circularity requirement that is becoming a global norm, echoing EU packaging and waste rules. Benchmarked against the EU, China is moving from voluntary to mandatory circular standards at scale, meaning suppliers must adapt formulations for two of the world's largest markets simultaneously. Early reformulation is a competitive advantage; late adaptation is a compliance risk.

China Daily | Chinatimes | China Economic Net — Packaging

item.title: Chinese carmakers outsold Japanese brands in Europe for the first time in May (138,400 vs 130,400 units); light-vehicle exports rose ~70% in Jan-May. China also exported CNY 20bn of robots, and McKinsey finds Chinese OEMs develop new vehicles in ~24 months, twice as fast.
item.description:
Chinese industrial competitiveness reached a symbolic threshold: in May, five Chinese carmakers sold 138,400 vehicles in Europe (+65% year-on-year), overtaking six Japanese brands (130,400, -3%) for the first time. China's light-vehicle exports rose about 70% in January-May to over 3.5 million units, with AlixPartners projecting 24.6 million total production and 10 million exports for 2026. A McKinsey study explains the underlying advantage: Chinese OEMs take a new EV from concept to launch in roughly 24 months, versus 40-50 elsewhere. In parallel, China exported 10.377 million robots worth nearly CNY 20 billion in five months (EU and ASEAN the top destinations), with industrial-robot output up 33.2% in Q1 — Bruegel and Goldman Sachs frame this as an overcapacity-driven competitiveness shift that is a primary cause of the EU's slowdown.

For chemical and ACS producers, the customer landscape is being redrawn. Chinese OEMs are becoming major buyers of automotive adhesives and coatings, and their compressed 24-month development cycles demand suppliers that can qualify materials far faster than legacy timelines allow — a capability, not just a pricing, challenge. Robotics scale-up simultaneously lifts demand for assembly adhesives and thermal materials. The strategic implication: Henkel must position with the rising Chinese OEM and robotics base while defending share with pressured incumbents. Benchmarked against the last decade, the speed of the share shift — visible now even in Europe's home market — is the critical new fact.

Commercial Times | South China Morning Post | China Economic Net — Autos | La Vanguardia — McKinsey | Global Times — Robots | South China Morning Post — Bruegel
